title: Family background; parents and siblings
description: Olive Weakley gives her maiden name Hardin, her nickname Ollie, and her birth in 1904 on a farm near Kamiah. She names her mother Fannie Elizabeth Mitchell, born in Kansas, and her father John Charles Hardin, born in Indiana, who farmed and ran the Tramway warehouse for forty-four years. She also names her one brother and two sisters.

title: Childhood farm life; neighborly cooperation; country doctors and telephones
description: Olive describes a happy, hard-working childhood on a small stock ranch where children picked berries, canned produce, made hay, and rode with the cattle. Neighbors exchanged work for woodcutting, butchering, and branding, and sat up with the sick, since doctors were few but dedicated, riding miles on horseback over muddy roads. Farmer-owned party-line telephone systems with a central at Widden connected the community cheaply.

title: Childhood play; Sunday visiting; first schoolhouse; the tramway
description: The children made toys from carrots, toothpicks, and broken dishes, swam in summer, and visited neighbors every Sunday, which her mother kept as a day of rest and dressing up. Olive attended a one-room log schoolhouse near Kamiah built by her father and Mr. Simner. She points out a picture of the tramway that carried grain from the Nez Perce Prairie to the railroad from about 1903 to 1944.

title: Becoming a teacher; lumber camp schools; destructive logging and the land's recovery
description: Olive went on to normal school and taught first at a summer school near Culdesac, then in a portable schoolhouse moved between Craig Mountain Lumber Company camps, snowbound with thirty students in winter. She recalls improvised playground equipment and the destructive donkey-engine logging of virgin timber. Visiting thirty years later, she was amazed at how the land had reforested itself.

title: Lewis and Clark canoe story questioned
description: Olive explains why she doubts the story that Lewis and Clark dug out Pine canoes in 1805, arguing pine would not float or be portable. She notes huge dead Cedars washed up around Canoe Camp, and concludes the canoes must have been hollowed from Cedar as the Indians did.

title: Teaching career; marriage and adopted son; wartime lookout work
description: Olive taught seventeen years, marrying at thirty because married women were barred from teaching. She met her widowed husband Ed, also a teacher, fell in love with his frail son first, and raised the boy as her own. The couple later taught as a husband-wife team near Orofino, and their teenage son manned a forest lookout while Ed served in World War II.

title: Courtship and marriage ideals; outdoor life; friends and grandchildren
description: Olive recalls a roughly year-long engagement and the goals she and Ed set, seeking security and a self-sustaining farm after the Depression. They shared outdoor recreation like steelheading and hunting, attended church, and built a life of honesty and friendship. Her seven grandchildren visit from Richmond and brought her comfort after Ed died.

title: Nez Perce berry buyers; pioneer hospitality
description: As a girl home alone with her sisters, Olive was frightened when about forty Nez Perce came to buy berries, speaking their language and packing handwoven baskets on their horses before fording the river. She then recalls her mother's pioneering insistence on feeding every visitor, a custom common among the isolated ranch families.

title: Parents' migration west; homestead hardships; the Depression
description: Her parents came west from Kansas in 1901, her father running a steam engine in the Palouse before settling a homestead near Kamiah. Her lonely young mother proved up the claim alone through winters while her father earned extra money and laid in winter supplies. Olive closes with the Depression, noting she lost five hundred dollars when the Kamiah bank closed.

title: Surviving the Great Depression; farm life and unemployment
description: Olive Weakley describes her early teaching salary in Keck and the financial hardships she faced during the Great Depression. She explains how her family survived by farming their own food, while unemployed men in Orofino built makeshift shelters, prompting local police intervention and the eventual creation of relief programs like the WPA.

title: Food preservation and canning
description: The conversation transitions to the present day as Olive Weakley discusses her busy schedule of drying prunes and canning. She offers the interviewer some of her home-dried prunes and explains her process for storing them in her freezer.
